claim: The body text of Guy's UPINT D11 'Egyptian fractions' section is exclusively about representing a SINGLE fraction (Rhind papyrus fractions, 4/n, 5/n, m/n Erdos-Straus/Sierpinski/Schinzel conjectures) as a sum of distinct unit fractions; it never discusses two independent triples sharing a common sum and a common sum of reciprocals.
stance_target: Section 5's problem being contained in D11
quoted_support: Dll Egyptian fractions. Some wit has suggested that Egyptian fractions, or unit fractions, are so called from the Hungarian for 'one'... This has suggested numerous problems, many of which are unsolved... Erdos & Straus conjectured that the equation 4/n = 1/x+1/y+1/z could be solved in positive integers for all n>1.

claim: Section D16's body text states the equal-sum-and-equal-product triples problem was fully solved by Schinzel (arbitrarily many triples possible), citing Schinzel's construction on the elliptic curve y^2=x^3-9x+9 (Cremona label 324C1, rank 1) and giving the smallest examples: 4 triples with common sum 118 -- (14,50,54),(15,40,63),(18,30,70),(21,25,72) -- and 4 triples with common product 25200 -- (6,56,75),(7,40,90),(9,28,100),(12,20,105).
stance_target: state of knowledge on the equal-sum-equal-product sibling problem (D16)
quoted_support: The problem to find as many different triples of positive integers as possible with the same sum and the same product has been solved by Schinzel: you can have arbitrarily many.

claim: Section D16 cites Schinzel, 'Triples of positive integers with the same sum and the same product,' Serdica Math. J. 22(1996) 587-588 (MR 98g:11033), as the paper that resolves the equal-sum-equal-product problem.
stance_target: primary reference for the equal-sum-equal-product problem
quoted_support: Andrzej Schinzel, Triples of positive integers with the same sum and the same product, Serdica Math. J., 22(1996) 587-588; MR 98g:11033.

claim: Section D28's body text identifies Mordell's reciprocal Diophantine equation as the single 4-variable equation 1/w+1/x+1/y+1/z+1/(wxyz)=0, distinct from a pairs-of-triples coincidence, and cites Longyear's n-variable generalization Sum(1/x_i)+Prod(1/x_i)=0.
stance_target: Section 5's problem being contained in D28
quoted_support: D28 A reciprocal diophantine equation. Mordell asked for the integer solutions of 1/w+1/x+1/y+1/z+1/(wxyz) = 0.

claim: An exhaustive grep of the full extracted text of Guy's UPINT 3rd edition (roughly 98,500 words, covering sections A through F and the Index of Authors Cited) for the phrases 'sum of the reciprocals', 'reciprocal sum', 'equal ... reciprocal', the digit sequences '2,8,8' and '3,3,12', and the terms 'triangle group', 'orbifold', 'covolume', and 'Takeuchi' returns zero hits relevant to (or matching at all, for the last four terms) Section 5's problem or the specific coincidence.
stance_target: presence of Section 5's problem or the (2,8,8)/(3,3,12) coincidence anywhere in Guy's UPINT
scope_conditions: full-text search of the entire book, 3rd ed. 2004
quoted_support: grep across the full extracted text for 'sum of the reciprocals', 'reciprocal sum', 'equal ... reciprocal' turns up only two unrelated hits (Brun's constant / twin primes; an Erdos-Graham-Ruzsa-Straus reciprocal-sum conjecture on primes not dividing binomial coefficients) -- NEITHER concerns pairs of integer triples.

claim: Guy's preface to the 3rd edition explicitly flags D16 (among others: B47, D2, D6, D8, D26, D27, D28, E15, F15, F17, F28) as a problem that has been 'largely or completely answered' since the 1st edition, corroborating that the equal-sum-equal-product problem is a settled/well-studied classical topic distinct from Section 5's open coincidence-counting problem.
stance_target: maturity of the equal-sum-equal-product literature relative to Section 5's problem
quoted_support: Problems which have been largely or completely answered are B47, D2, D6, D8, D16, D26, D27, D28, E15, F15, Fl7 & F28.
